sources.content:
## Danger signals during pregnancy
The booklet lists vaginal bleeding, convulsions, fever and severe abdominal pain among pregnancy danger signals. It advises seeking help immediately if complications occur. This older 2012 booklet is a source pointer, not a complete or current triage protocol.

sources.title: Keeping well during pregnancy and after childbirth
sources.license_note: WHO web content; verify applicable permissions and terms before redistribution.
sources.content:
## When to seek support
WHO's public guidance encourages contacting a health worker for danger signs such as bleeding, severe headache or abdominal pain. It also advises seeking support for intense sadness, anxiety, exhaustion, inability to cope, or thoughts of harming oneself or the baby. This summary is educational and does not assess an individual's symptoms.

sources.title: WHO recommendations on antenatal care for a positive pregnancy experience
sources.version: WHO/RHR/16.12; guideline page lists later updates
sources.license_note: WHO guideline page states CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IGO; commercial use requires permission. Verify current terms before redistribution.
sources.content:
## Scope of antenatal care
WHO's antenatal-care guideline covers health promotion, prevention, maternal and fetal assessment, nutrition, and interventions for common physiological symptoms. Its nutrition recommendations include iron and folic-acid supplementation as part of antenatal care; an individual plan and dose must come from a qualified clinician and current local guidance. The guideline page lists updates to some recommendations after the 2016 publication.

sources.title: Infant and young child feeding
sources.license_note: WHO web content; verify applicable permissions and terms before redistribution.
sources.content:
## Breastfeeding recommendations
WHO and UNICEF recommend starting breastfeeding within one hour after birth and exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, followed by continued breastfeeding with suitable complementary foods. Families may need individualized support; this general summary does not replace advice for a particular mother or infant.

sources.title: Anaemia
sources.license_note: WHO web content; verify applicable permissions and terms before redistribution.
sources.content:
## Iron-rich foods and anaemia
WHO notes that anaemia can have multiple causes and is assessed using blood haemoglobin, so a food diary cannot diagnose it. Its public information names legumes such as lentils and beans, fortified cereals, and dark green leafy vegetables as iron-containing foods. Vitamin C-rich fruit and vegetables can help the body absorb iron from food. These are general food examples, not a treatment plan.

sources.title: Nutrition counselling during pregnancy
sources.license_note: WHO web content; verify applicable permissions and terms before redistribution.
sources.content:
## Food variety in pregnancy
WHO guidance describes pregnancy nutrition counselling as supporting a varied diet with adequate energy, protein, vitamins and minerals. Food examples include vegetables, beans, nuts, fruit, and pasteurized dairy; suitability depends on the person's preferences and circumstances. Individual clinical instructions take priority.

sources.license_note: Government web content; verify reuse terms before redistribution. Page also contains programme supplement schedules that are intentionally not reproduced in this summary.
sources.content:
## Anaemia Mukt Bharat and dietary variety
The NHM describes Anaemia Mukt Bharat as a life-cycle programme that includes pregnant and lactating women. Its public page also calls for dietary diversification and greater intake of iron-rich, protein-rich, and vitamin C-rich foods. The programme page contains supplement schedules; this summary does not provide a dose or personal treatment advice.

sources.content:
## Postpartum and newborn counselling
The manual covers early breastfeeding support and describes maternal danger signs after delivery that should prompt urgent facility care, including excessive bleeding, convulsions, difficult breathing, and severe headache with blurred vision. It also discusses newborn counselling. This summary is not a complete protocol; follow current local clinical advice.

sources.content:
## Emergency number in India
The Government of India's Emergency Response Support System describes 112 as a pan-India number for emergency assistance, including health emergencies. Availability and response can depend on local circumstances; outside India, contact local emergency services.
